content:
A short post on social media puts a familiar charge in a few lines. Islam, it says, grew out of a "gnostic unitarian arianistic Christian cult", these "streams of thought" were "refuted in 325, 431 and 525", and John of Damascus refuted them again "in 649" in his work on "the heresy of the Ishmaelites". The conclusion is that Islam is a Christian heresy that the church settled long ago.

The charge has a real starting point. John of Damascus did class Islam among the heresies, and he did say that Muhammad (peace be upon him) seemed to have met an Arian monk. This article aims to provide context to the charge, insha'Allah, in seven answers: what the three labels mean, what the dates show, what the councils settled, what John of Damascus wrote and how well he knew the Quran, and where the Quran stands.

The Quran states its own position in four verses: "Say: He is God, One. God, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born. Nor is there to Him any equivalent" (112:1-4).[1] Every answer below is measured against that.

The three labels cannot all describe one religion, because they contradict one another. The gnostic teachers of the second century set the God of Jesus apart from a lesser maker of the world, whom some of them called ignorant or arrogant. We set out their teaching, and Marcion's, in our article on early Christians who called the creator evil.

The Quran says the opposite of every gnostic claim. The Creator is the one God, "who perfected everything He created" (32:7), and the creation is no mistake: "We did not create the heaven and the earth and whatever is between them in vain" (38:27).[1]

The gnostic teachers also taught contempt for the body and for the world it lives in. The Quran rebukes that contempt by name: "Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?" (7:32).[1]

"Unitarian", as the name of a movement, belongs to sixteenth-century Europe, nine centuries after the Quran. A word coined for later Christians cannot name the source of an earlier book.

Arius, a priest of Alexandria, taught that the Son was begotten by the Father before all things, and that "there was a time when the Son was not", as the church historian Socrates reports his words. On his view the Son was the first creature, made before the world and given a rank above it.[2]

The Quran's Jesus has no such rank. "The likeness of Jesus before God is that of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him 'Be', and he was" (3:59). He is a man born of Mary in history, "a messenger" like the messengers before him, who "used to eat food" (5:75).[3]

Arius also kept the Son as the one through whom God made everything else. The Quran gives creation no intermediary of that kind: "Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be', and it is" (2:117). The same word "Be" made Adam and made Jesus.

The Quran also rules out every form of worship given to him. Jesus himself says on the Day of Judgement that he told people only to "worship God, my Lord and your Lord" (5:117). A religion that denies the Son any existence before Mary, and forbids all worship of him, is no form of Arianism.[3]

The first two dates are real. The council of Nicaea met in 325 and condemned Arius. The council of Ephesus met in 431 and condemned Nestorius, a bishop of Constantinople who held the Trinity and objected to calling Mary the "Mother of God".[4]

Ephesus therefore settled a dispute between two parties that both confessed the Trinity. Whatever it decided, it decided nothing about a religion that denies the Trinity, and nothing about a book that was not yet revealed.

No council met in 525. The next council the churches count as ecumenical, the second council of Constantinople, met in 553 to condemn the "Three Chapters", writings judged too close to Nestorius.[4]

None of these councils discussed Islam, which did not yet exist. The council of 553 met seventeen years before the Prophet's birth, by the usual dating, so it cannot have "refuted" anything he taught.

The councils settled which party held the field in a given decade, and the field changed. In 359 the emperor Constantius II called the western bishops to Ariminum, modern Rimini. The council first stood by the creed of Nicaea, and then its envoys accepted a creed acceptable to the Arian party, and the bishops who remained were pressed to sign it.[5]

Jerome, writing a generation later, described the result in one sentence: "the Nicene Faith stood condemned by acclamation. The whole world groaned, and was astonished to find itself Arian." A doctrine "refuted" in 325 had won a council of its own within thirty-four years.[5]

A vote, however large, does not tell us what Jesus taught. For that the Gospels are the witness, and in them Jesus prays to "the only true God" and speaks of "my Father and your Father, my God and your God" (John 17:3; 20:17). We follow that thread in our article Did Jesus pray, and to whom?.[6]

John of Damascus was born around 675 and died in 749, so he wrote nothing in 649. He lived under the Umayyad caliphs, and his father served in their administration in Damascus. His chapter on the "Ishmaelites" stands near the end of his catalogue of heresies.[7]

His account of the Prophet's sources is a guess, and he says so. Muhammad, he writes, came upon the Old and New Testaments "and likewise, it seems, having conversed with an Arian monk, devised his own heresy". The words "it seems" carry the whole of the "Arian" charge, and John names no source for it.[8]

John also records what the Muslims of his day answered: "they call us Hetaeriasts, or Associators, because, they say, we introduce an associate with God by declaring Christ to the Son of God and God." That is the Quran's own charge (5:72-73), and it was the Muslim reply already in the eighth century.[8]

John's own summary of Muslim belief also tells against the "Arian" label. He writes that Muhammad "says that there is one God, creator of all things, who has neither been begotten nor has begotten", and that Christ is "a creature and a servant". Arius taught that the Father begot the Son before all things; John's Muslims deny that God begets at all.[8]

John writes about the Quran as a book divided into "books" with titles, and some of what he reports is there: the chapters he calls "The Woman", "The Table" and "The Heifer" are the fourth, fifth and second surahs. Other things he reports are not in it at all.[8]

He describes a "book of The Camel of God", and his own modern translator marks the title in a footnote: "Not in the Koran." The Quran does tell of the she-camel sent to the people of Thamud, with a share of the water on alternate days (7:73; 26:155). John's version adds what the Quran never says: that she drank the whole river, was too large to pass between two mountains, and left a calf that God took up to Himself.

He says that the Quran allows "a thousand concubines" and requires a divorced wife to marry her husband's brother. The Quran contains neither rule.[8]

John is a witness to what some Christians in Damascus said about Islam a century after the Prophet. He is a poor witness to the text of the Quran, and a chapter that mixes the Quran with tales that are not in it cannot settle what the Quran teaches.

The Quran does not take a side in the Christian debate over how the Son relates to the Father. It rejects the question's premise: "It is not for God to take a son. Exalted is He" (19:35). "Do not say: Three. Desist; it is better for you. God is only one God" (4:171).[9]

That answer rejects the Nicene Son, who is "of one substance" with the Father, and it rejects the Arian Son, the first and highest creature, through whom the world was made. In the Quran the world was made by God's command alone, "Be", and Jesus himself came into being by that command (3:59).[9]

In al-Faruqi's statement of tawhid, Creator and creature are two orders of being, and "it is forever impossible that the one be united with, infused, confused with or diffused into the other." Arianism blurred that line by placing a creature above creation; Nicaea blurred it by calling a man God. The Quran keeps it.[10]

The bottom line

The post gives three labels that contradict one another and four dates, of which two are real, one names a year without a council, and one is wrong by a century. The councils it cites were votes, and one of them was overturned within a generation, as Jerome records.

John of Damascus is the source of the "Arian" charge, and he offered it as a guess, "it seems". His own summary of Muslim belief, a God who "has neither been begotten nor has begotten", contradicts it, and his account of the Quran includes chapters and laws the Quran does not contain. He also preserved the Muslim answer of his own day: that Christians had set an associate beside God.

The Quran answers Arius and Nicaea alike, with the God who "neither begets nor is born" (112:3). God knows best.

Notes

  1. Quran 112:1–4; 32:7; 38:27; 7:32.
  2. Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History 1.5, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 2, translated by A. C. Zenos (1890).
  3. Quran 3:59; 5:75; 2:117; 5:116–117.
  4. Norman P. Tanner (ed.), Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils, vol. 1 (London: Sheed and Ward; Washington: Georgetown University Press, 1990), on Nicaea (325), Ephesus (431) and Constantinople II (553).
  5. Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians 17–19, on the council of Ariminum (359) under Constantius II, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 6, translated by W. H. Fremantle (1893).
  6. John 17:3; 20:17. Bible quotations follow the English Standard Version.
  7. Sidney H. Griffith, "John of Damascus and the Church in Syria in the Umayyad Era: The Intellectual and Cultural Milieu of Orthodox Christians in the World of Islam", Hugoye: Journal of Syriac Studies 11.1 (2008).
  8. John of Damascus, On Heresies 100, in Saint John of Damascus: Writings, translated by Frederic H. Chase, The Fathers of the Church 37 (Washington: Catholic University of America Press, 1958), pp. 153–160, with the translator's notes; compare Quran 4:3, 2:230, 7:73 and 26:155–158.
  9. Quran 19:35; 4:171; 3:59.
  10. Ismail Raji al-Faruqi, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd edition (Herndon: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 1.
